description: The classic data structures and algorithm design techniques, each analysed for correctness and running time and implemented in C++ with tests. Taught to the depth of a leading algorithms course.
modelledOn: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms
Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis in C++
outcomes: Specify abstract data types and implement them in C++ with clear interfaces, invariants and tests.
Analyse the time and space complexity of iterative and recursive algorithms, including amortised analysis.
Implement and choose among lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, balanced trees, heaps and graphs.
Implement and compare sorting and searching algorithms and justify their bounds.
Apply greedy, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, randomised and backtracking techniques to new problems.
Solve graph problems with BFS, DFS, shortest paths, minimum spanning trees and topological sort.

units.title: Data structures, abstract data types and analysis of algorithms
topics: Abstract data types versus implementations; interfaces, invariants and encapsulation in C++ classes and templates
Models of computation; counting operations; best, worst and average case
Asymptotic notation: O, Omega, Theta; growth rates and limits
Analysing loops and nested loops; recurrences and the master theorem
Amortised analysis: dynamic arrays and the aggregate and accounting methods
Measuring running time experimentally and comparing with theory

units.title: Lists, stacks and queues
topics: Array lists and dynamic resizing; singly, doubly and circular linked lists; iterators
Stacks: array and linked implementations; expression evaluation, balanced brackets, undo
Queues and deques; circular buffers; priority queue as an ADT
The C++ STL: vector, list, deque, stack, queue and their complexity guarantees

units.title: Recursion
topics: Recursive thinking and the call stack; base cases and progress
Recursion versus iteration; tail recursion; memoisation
Classic problems: permutations, subsets, Tower of Hanoi, flood fill, binary search
Proving recursive algorithms correct by induction

units.title: Sorting
topics: Insertion, selection and bubble sort; stability and in-place sorting
Merge sort and quicksort: analysis, pivot choice, randomised quicksort
Heaps and heapsort; the binary heap as a priority queue
Lower bound for comparison sorting; counting sort, radix sort, bucket sort
Choosing a sort: std::sort, introsort and when each algorithm wins

units.title: Searching and hashing
topics: Linear and binary search; interpolation search; order statistics and quickselect
Hash functions, uniform hashing, universal hashing
Collision resolution: chaining, open addressing (linear, quadratic, double hashing); load factor and rehashing
Hash tables in practice: unordered_map, string hashing, Bloom filters
Applications: dictionaries, counting, deduplication, caching

units.title: Trees
topics: Tree terminology; binary trees and traversals (preorder, inorder, postorder, level order)
Binary search trees: search, insert, delete; expected height
Balanced trees: AVL rotations; red-black trees; 2-3 trees and B-trees for disks
Tries and suffix trees for strings; Huffman coding trees
Augmented trees: order statistics, interval trees; segment trees and Fenwick trees
std::map and std::set and their guarantees

units.title: Graphs
topics: Graph representations: adjacency matrix and list; weighted and directed graphs
Breadth-first and depth-first search; connected components; cycle detection
Topological sort and DAGs; strongly connected components
Shortest paths: Dijkstra with a heap, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall; the tro-tro route problem
Minimum spanning trees: Kruskal with union-find, Prim
Network flow in brief: Ford-Fulkerson and bipartite matching

units.title: Design techniques
topics: Greedy: activity selection, fractional knapsack, Huffman, interval scheduling; proving greedy choices
Divide-and-conquer: closest pair, Karatsuba multiplication, Strassen in brief
Dynamic programming: 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, edit distance, matrix chain, coin change in cedis
Randomised algorithms: randomised quicksort, hashing, Monte Carlo and Las Vegas
Backtracking and branch-and-bound: N-queens, sudoku, subset sum
Introduction to NP-completeness and what to do when no fast algorithm is known
